newsitem.title: USA: Fashion industry welcomes Clinton drug message.
newsitem.headline: Fashion industry welcomes Clinton drug message.

text.p: Leaders in the high-fashion world agreed on Wednesday with President Bill Clinton's view that the industry has glamorized drug use, but some suggested that the decadent look is already on its way out.

Magazines and modelling layouts have at times gone too far in portraying what Clinton called the "allure of heroin," but those days are over, said Patrick McCarthy, chairman and editorial director of "W" and "Women's Wear Daily," two influential publications in the fashion industry.
"People got carried away by the glamour of decadence, and editors were not paying enough attention and art designers were not paying enough attention," he said.
With growing attention from the public and now the president's message, "Nobody can pretend ignorance now," he said.
"If you start putting out stories and photos that in any way suggest you support drug use, people come down on you really hard. Commercially, you're going to suffer," he said.
Besides, the drug look has already met the fate of most fashion trends, he said.
"It's been done so much," he said. "Not only is it bad, it's boring. That is really what kills in fashion -- when it's really boring."
Katie Ford, head of Ford Models Inc., whose top models include Christie Brinkley, Jerry Hall and Rachel Hunter, agreed that while the look might be passe, the problem remains.
"The look died, but the problem didn't," she said. "It's a societal problem that needs to be fixed."
Advertising columnist Barbara Lippert, who writes for New York magazine, cautioned that the president should not point blame just at the fashion industry but consider the broader popular culture.
"It's very simplistic to point fingers," she said.

But advertisers are forced to become more and more outrageous to get attention, she said. Thus fashion models appear with deathly pallors, shredded clothing, lifeless poses and needle tracks up their arms.

"In this media culture, there's been every sex act and every tattoo and every piercing possible and they have to keep getting more and more extreme until they get to death," she said. "Now they've done death."
Such extreme images are a natural outgrowth of cutting edge fashion, the experts said.

"Fashion photographers want to create pictures that are different from what's out there," McCarthy said, but added, "Very few people go out and decide to do an ad campaign or a photo layout encouraging people to take heroin. They don't do it deliberately."
The president's message makes life easier, said John Casablancas, head of Elite Model Management that handles stars such as Linda Evangelista and Claudia Schiffer.

"I've seen hundreds of careers destroyed, our relationship with some top models destroyed ... and we nevertheless did not say anything," he said. "We didn't want to antagonize anybody, and you don't want to seem like you're old-fashioned."
"This gives us the opportunity to be more brave and to say, 'the heck with it,'" he said. "It'll cost me a couple of clients but never mind."
